**GLANDERSWATCH**

**Zoonotic Disease Risk Intelligence & Early-Warning Platform**

ML Risk Prediction, RAG-Based Explanations and Farmer/Equine-Owner Alerts

*Project Proposal • India-first, global-data perspective • Glanders as the first case study*

# **1\. Project overview**

Glanders is a notifiable, contagious and potentially fatal disease of horses, donkeys and mules caused by Burkholderia mallei. India’s revised 2025 National Action Plan describes the disease as zoonotic and notes that asymptomatic infected equids can remain infectious. India had 5.44 lakh equids in the 2019 Livestock Census, many of them in unorganized livelihood sectors such as transport, construction, brick kilns, tourism and pilgrimage. \[1\]

National surveillance demonstrates a substantial, geographically distributed problem: 158,798 equid serum samples from 391 districts in 19 states and three Union Territories were screened during 2019–2023; 728 seropositive equids were identified in 138 districts. Uttar Pradesh accounted for about 60% of positives. \[2\]

GlandersWatch turns this surveillance context into a full-stack software platform: a machine-learning risk engine, a retrieval-augmented explanation layer grounded in official guidance, a web dashboard, and an SMS/WhatsApp alert service. The architecture is disease-agnostic; glanders is the initial case study.

# **2\. Proposed idea**

Build a platform that learns from historical glanders occurrence, equine population, geography and environmental conditions to estimate the probability of a future glanders event for a geographic/time unit. The prediction is then (a) shown on a geospatial risk map, (b) explained in plain language with citations to official documents through a RAG assistant, and (c) passed to an alert service so registered equine owners or field workers receive a concise warning by SMS or WhatsApp.

The system is a risk-forecasting tool, not an animal-diagnosis system.

## **Core pipeline**

Disease history \+ Weather \+ Geography \+ Equine population  
                    \|  
             ML Risk Engine  (XGBoost / LightGBM, calibrated)  
                    \|  
   Risk probability per district / month  
        \|                    \|                    \|  
   Risk map & dashboard   RAG explanation   SMS / WhatsApp alerts  
                          (LLM \+ citations)  
					(Shaktimayee)		(Shanmukh)

# **3\. Why this disease**

| Criterion | Evidence |
| :---- | :---- |
| India relevance | 158,798 samples; 728 seropositive equids; 138 affected districts, 2019–2023. \[2\] |
| International relevance | Glanders remains endemic/reported in parts of Africa, Asia, the Middle East and Central/South America. \[3\] |
| Economic/livelihood relevance | 5.44 lakh equids in India; unorganized equids support livelihoods in transport, construction, brick kilns, tourism and pilgrimage. \[1\] |
| Data availability | WOAH WAHIS provides public animal-health data from 2005 onward and supports disease/country/species filtering and export. \[4\] India also has an open-government historical livestock-disease dataset covering 2005–2011 and explicitly including Glanders. \[5\] |
| Existing-system gap | ICAR-NIVEDI NADRES disease catalogue lists multiple livestock diseases but does not list Glanders; its system already provides AI disease forecasting for other diseases. \[6\] |
| ML gap | The ML literature located for Glanders includes laboratory identification using Raman spectroscopy, not a comparable geographic/time outbreak-risk forecasting application. \[7\] |
| Explainability gap | Risk scores alone are hard for field workers to act on. Linking each prediction to official control guidance (National Action Plan, WOAH) through cited explanations is the platform’s added contribution. |

# **4\. Existing work**

* India has long-running statutory surveillance. Historical Indian surveillance reported 1,145 positive equids among 128,404 sera tested during 2006–2018. \[8\]

* Recent national surveillance covers 2019–2023 and identifies strong geographic and seasonal variation. \[2\]

* WOAH WAHIS provides the global official reporting infrastructure and public data. \[4\]

* Machine learning has been used for laboratory identification of B. mallei using Raman spectra, but that is a diagnostic spectroscopy problem rather than a population-level forecasting problem. \[7\]

* NADRES v2 is an established Indian livestock early-warning system and is treated as an existing benchmark; its current forecast list does not include Glanders. \[6\]

# **5\. Data sources**

Only sources that are publicly accessible or have a documented public-access route are included as core inputs. The project does not depend on an unpublished institutional database.

| Dataset | What it provides | Role in platform |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| WOAH WAHIS | Official disease events and monitoring data; disease, species, geography, dates; outbreaks, susceptible, cases, deaths and vaccination fields. | Primary global outcome/history data |
| India OGD: Incidence of Livestock Diseases in India | Outbreaks, attacks and deaths for Indian livestock diseases, 2005–2011; Glanders explicitly included. | India baseline/training source \+ validation |
| DAHD National Action Plan for Glanders, 2025 | Equine population, surveillance/control framework, case definitions, surveillance plan and state-level context. | India features, context, alert guidance; RAG knowledge base |
| 20th Livestock Census | Indian equine population; 5.44 lakh horses/ponies, donkeys and mules in 2019\. | Exposure denominator |
| ERA5-Land | Global hourly meteorological variables from 1950 onward. | Weather covariates |
| FAO GLW4 | Global gridded livestock populations. | Equine-density proxy / livestock context |
| Administrative boundaries | Country/state/district geometries. | Spatial joins, map layers |
| Public guidance documents | WOAH/WHO disease sheets, DAHD/ICAR guidelines, open-access research papers. | RAG knowledge base (Section 13\) |

# **6\. Data that is actually usable immediately**

**India historical core:** the Government of India’s OGD catalog states that its dataset contains the number of outbreaks, attacks and deaths for livestock diseases from 2005–2011 and names Glanders among the diseases. The catalog exposes a Catalog API and Zip Download. \[5\]

**Global/current core:** WOAH states that WAHIS contains validated data since 2005, that the public interface is unrestricted for analysis, and that its enhanced filtering/data-extraction functions allow information to be exported in multiple formats. \[4\]

# **7\. Training dataset construction**

| Input group | Example variables | Source |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Disease history | Outbreak count, attacks/cases, deaths; lagged 1/3/6/12-month or reporting-period counts | WAHIS \+ India OGD |
| Geography | State/district/country, latitude/longitude where available, distance to recent event, neighbouring-area activity | WAHIS \+ boundaries |
| Equine exposure | Equine population/density | 20th Livestock Census \+ spatial layers |
| Weather | Temperature, precipitation, humidity-related variables, seasonal aggregates | ERA5-Land |
| Temporal | Month, season, year, recent trend (derived) | Derived |
| Target | Outbreak reported in the next prediction period: 0/1, derived from future WAHIS/OGD observation | WAHIS/OGD |

# **8\. Data engineering and cleaning**

* Scheduled ingestion (Airflow or Prefect) from WAHIS, OGD and ERA5-Land into PostgreSQL/PostGIS; datasets versioned with DVC.

* Standardize disease names and geographic names.

* Remove duplicate event/report records while retaining legitimate follow-up reports.

* Normalize dates and convert reporting periods into a common time index.

* Validate coordinates and assign events to administrative units.

* Aggregate events into geographic-time units.

* Generate lagged outbreak features using only information available before the prediction date.

* Handle missing values explicitly; do not convert missing surveillance into disease absence.

* Automated data-quality checks (Great Expectations) on every ingestion run.

* Create chronological train/validation/test splits before model fitting.

# **9\. Machine-learning problem**

**Input:** for each geographic unit and prediction date: historical glanders activity \+ equine exposure \+ geography \+ weather \+ seasonality \+ recent spatial outbreak activity.

**Output:** a calibrated probability of at least one reported glanders event in the next prediction period. The initial implementation uses a monthly prediction window where the available temporal resolution supports it; otherwise it uses the reporting period available in the source.

# **10\. ML workflow**

WAHIS / India OGD / ERA5-Land  
        \|  
Cleaning \+ geographic/time aggregation  (PostGIS)  
        \|  
Lagged outbreak \+ weather \+ equine \+ spatial features  
        \|  
Leakage-safe temporal split  
        \|  
Logistic Regression \-\> Random Forest \-\> XGBoost \-\> LightGBM  
        \|  
Imbalance handling \+ probability calibration  
        \|  
SHAP explanations \+ MLflow tracking / model registry  
        \|  
Risk threshold \-\> Alert service \+ RAG explanation

# **11\. Models and experiments**

| Model / technique | Purpose |
| :---- | :---- |
| Logistic Regression | Interpretable baseline |
| Random Forest | Nonlinear tabular baseline |
| XGBoost | Boosted-tree model for nonlinear interactions |
| LightGBM | Efficient boosted-tree comparison |
| Class weights / focal loss / resampling | Handle rare-event imbalance (resampling applied inside training folds only) |
| Probability calibration (Platt / isotonic) | Produces usable probabilities for alert thresholds |
| SHAP | Per-district feature attribution; feeds the explanation layer |
| MLflow | Experiment tracking, metrics comparison and model registry |

# **12\. Evaluation**

## **12.1 Prediction model**

* ROC-AUC and PR-AUC for ranking performance.

* Precision, recall/sensitivity, specificity and F1 at the chosen alert threshold.

* Brier score/calibration curve to determine whether predicted probabilities are meaningful.

* Temporal holdout as the primary test: later periods must remain unseen during training.

* Geographic holdout where the sample size permits.

* Ablation tests: outbreak history only; weather only; equine exposure only; combined features.

* Alert-level evaluation: missed events versus false alerts, because unnecessary warnings can cause alert fatigue.

## **12.2 RAG explanation layer (Shaktimayee)**

* Retrieval quality: recall@k on a hand-built question set.

* Faithfulness and answer relevance (e.g. RAGAS), with manual review of a sample.

* Citation check: every claim in an explanation must trace to a retrieved passage.

# **13\. RAG explanation and guidance layer (Shaktimayee)**

This layer answers questions such as “Why is this district high risk?” and “What should owners do?”. It combines the model’s own outputs with retrieved official guidance, so the LLM never invents advice.

User question  
      \|  
      v  
Retrieval  
(pgvector, hybrid search  
 \+ reranking over guidance docs)  
      \|  
      v  
Context \=  
  retrieved passages  
  \+ district risk score  
  \+ top SHAP factors  
      \|  
      v  
LLM answer  
  with citations  
  \+ preventive action  
      \|  
      v  
Guardrails:  
  answer only from context;  
  "population-level forecast,  
   not a diagnosis"

* **Knowledge base:** DAHD National Action Plan, WOAH/WHO disease information, ICAR and open-access research papers, movement-control and quarantine guidance.

* **Models:** open-source embeddings (sentence-transformers); LLM via a local model (Ollama) or a free-tier API, chosen behind a swappable interface.

* **Safety:** refuses to diagnose individual animals; refuses to answer outside retrieved sources; always shows source citations.

# **14\. Farmer / equine-owner alert system (Shanmukh)**

The primary user interaction for owners is a notification, not a web application. A web dashboard is retained for administrators, researchers and veterinary personnel.

Prediction job finishes (Celery beat → writes predictions table)  
        │  event: "predictions\_ready"  
        ▼  
1\. Alert Evaluator ── for each area that has registered users:  
        │   reads latest prediction \+ that area's previous alert state  
        ▼  
2\. Rules Engine  
        ├─ Threshold      → probability → LOW / MEDIUM / HIGH  
        ├─ Suppression    → should we send anything at all?  
        └─ Deduplication  → have we already sent this?  
        ▼  
3\. Alert record created (alerts table, unique key)  
        ▼  
4\. Fan-out → one notification job per subscription (Redis queue)  
        ▼  
5\. Notification Service  
        ├─ Template renderer (language: users choice)  
        ├─ Channel adapters: SMS \| WhatsApp \| Telegram  
        ├─ Retries with backoff  
        └─ Delivery status webhooks → alert\_delivery\_logs  
        ▼  
Owner / field worker receives: risk  (short action \+ vet contact from RAG (done by user))  
        ▼  
Admin dashboard: alert history, delivery status, failures

* Alerts available in English and Hindi, extendable to other regional languages.

![][image1]

### **The three important rules :**

**1\. Threshold**

* Map the calibrated probability to levels. The values should come from the ML team’s validation results (precision vs. recall at the alert level), not a default 0.5.  
* Make thresholds **configurable**, not hard-coded.  
* Use **hysteresis**: enter HIGH at ≥ T, but only leave HIGH when the probability drops below T minus a margin. This stops flickering around the boundary.  
* Optionally require the risk to be elevated for N consecutive periods before escalating.

**2\. Suppression** (decides whether to send at all)

* Send only on a **state change** (e.g. MEDIUM→HIGH), not every month while the level stays the same.  
* **Cooldown** per area and level (e.g. no repeated HIGH within N days), but an **escalation bypasses** it.  
* Per-user daily cap, and **quiet hours** so nothing goes out at night.  
* **Stale-data guard**: if the data-freshness check fails, don’t alert on old data. Notify the admin instead.  
* An admin **manual mute/override** for an area.  
* Optionally, a short “risk reduced” message on de-escalation.

**3\. Deduplication** (prevents the same alert twice)

* An **alert-level idempotency key**: `(area_id, prediction_period, level)` with a unique DB constraint. Re-running a job or retraining the model can’t create a second alert for the same period.  
* A **recipient-level key**: `(alert_id, subscription_id)`.  
* A **send-level check**: before each send or retry, check the delivery log, so a retry after a timeout doesn’t double-send.

# **15\. Software architecture**

| Layer | Technology / role |
| :---- | :---- |
| Data pipeline | Python, pandas, GeoPandas; Airflow/Prefect scheduled WAHIS/OGD/ERA5 ingestion; Great Expectations; DVC |
| ML pipeline | scikit-learn, XGBoost, LightGBM, SHAP; MLflow tracking and registry |
| RAG service | sentence-transformers, pgvector, reranker, LLM (Ollama or free-tier API) |
| Backend API | FastAPI (REST), JWT authentication, role-based access, Pydantic validation |
| Task queue / scheduler | Celery \+ Redis (prediction, alert and retraining jobs) |
| Storage | PostgreSQL/PostGIS for areas, subscriptions, predictions, alert logs; pgvector for document embeddings |
| Notifications | SMS (SNS/Twilio), WhatsApp Business Cloud API, Telegram bot for free demo |
| Frontend | Next.js \+ TypeScript, MapLibre/Leaflet, chart library, Tailwind CSS |
| Deployment | Docker Compose; optional cloud deployment (AWS or free-tier alternative) |
| CI/CD & monitoring | GitHub Actions, pytest, Prometheus \+ Grafana, Evidently (data/model drift) |

# **^Shanmukh and Shaktimayee**

# **16\. Full-stack application (^Shanmukh and Shaktimayee)**

## **16.1 Backend (FastAPI)**

* Endpoints: /predict, /risk-map, /districts/{id}/explain, /chat, /subscribe, /alerts, /models.

* Auth with JWT and three roles: admin, veterinary officer, owner/field worker.

* Background workers for scheduled predictions, alert dispatch with retries, and periodic retraining.

## **16.2 Frontend (Next.js \+ TypeScript)**

* **Risk map:** district-level choropleth with a time slider and risk-level filters.

* **District detail:** risk score, trend, top contributing factors (SHAP), and recent alerts.

* **Ask-why chat:** RAG assistant with visible citations to source documents.

* **Admin panel:** model metrics, experiment comparison, alert history and delivery status, data-freshness indicators.

* **Subscription page:** owners register phone, area and language.

## **16.3 Data model (core tables)**

areas (PostGIS geometry), observations, features, predictions, model\_versions, documents/chunks (pgvector), users, subscriptions, alerts, alert\_delivery\_logs.

# **17\. MLOps and DevOps**

* Experiment tracking and model registry with MLflow; every deployed model traceable to data version and code commit.

* CI/CD with GitHub Actions: linting, unit tests (pytest), API tests, container build.

* Containerised services (API, worker, database, Redis, frontend) orchestrated with Docker Compose.

* Monitoring: API metrics and logs (Prometheus \+ Grafana); data and prediction drift reports (Evidently).

* Scheduled retraining and comparison against the current champion model before promotion.

# **18\. Example outputs**

## **18.1 Alert message (Shanmukh)**

GLANDERS RISK ALERT  
Elevated glanders risk has been predicted for your registered area  
for the next prediction period.  
Risk: HIGH  
Reason: recent reported activity and environmental/geographic risk factors.  
Action: avoid unnecessary movement or mixing of equids and contact the  
local veterinary authority if an animal is suspected of illness.  
This is a population-level risk forecast and is not a diagnosis.

## **18.2 Example RAG explanation (Shaktimayee)**

Question: “Why is District X rated HIGH this month?”

Answer (illustrative): “Risk is elevated mainly because of recent reported activity in neighbouring districts and the district’s high equine density. The National Action Plan recommends movement control and quarantine of suspected cases \[source: DAHD Action Plan, sec. X\]. This is a population-level forecast, not a diagnosis.”

# **19\. Why the alert is useful**

* Many Indian equids are kept in unorganized sectors for livelihood activities, where management and movement patterns differ from controlled establishments. \[1\]

* India’s 2025 National Action Plan specifically emphasizes surveillance, movement control, quarantine and public awareness. \[1\]

* An automated warning can translate a geographic risk model into a message that reaches an owner without requiring the owner to operate a dashboard.

# **20\. Existing Indian system and differentiation**

| Existing system | Status | Project distinction |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| ICAR-NIVEDI NADRES v2 | AI livestock disease forewarning with up to two months advance prediction; current disease list does not include Glanders. \[6\] | Glanders-specific model using public WAHIS \+ Indian OGD, transparent feature construction, cited explanations and reproducible experiments. |
| WOAH WAHIS | Official global disease reporting/monitoring and public information system. \[4\] | Uses WAHIS as the data source; does not replace official reporting. |
| Indian National Action Plan | Existing statutory glanders surveillance/control programme. \[1\] | Software forecasting/alert layer is an academic prototype and not a substitute for statutory surveillance; the Plan is used as the guidance source for the RAG layer. |

# **21\. Farmer benefit and project scope**

| Problem | System response |
| :---- | :---- |
| Disease information is spread across surveillance and veterinary systems. | Convert model output into a simple location-specific alert and a single map. |
| Farmers/owners may not use a dashboard. | SMS/WhatsApp-first interaction. |
| Glanders is rare enough that indiscriminate warnings create noise. | Threshold \+ suppression \+ calibrated probability. |
| Movement can contribute to spread. | Alert includes official movement-control guidance. |
| A risk score can be misunderstood as diagnosis. | Every alert and explanation states that it is a population-level forecast. |
| Officers need to know why an area is high risk. | Cited RAG explanations plus SHAP factors. |

# **25\. Limitations**

* WAHIS is surveillance data and therefore reflects reporting practices; absence of a report does not prove absence of disease.

* The Indian OGD dataset covers 2005–2011, so it is historical and must not be presented as current surveillance.

* The 2019–2023 national serosurvey is an important Indian validation/context source, but its full individual-level raw data are not claimed as an open training file.

* Glanders is rare, so class imbalance and limited event counts may constrain fine-grained geographic prediction.

* Environmental variables can support risk estimation but do not establish causation.

* LLM explanations can be wrong; they are constrained to retrieved sources, cited, and evaluated, but are advisory only.

# **26\. Expected project outcome**

The final system will demonstrate that publicly accessible animal-health data can be transformed into a reproducible glanders risk-forecasting pipeline, explained through cited official guidance, and delivered as a practical full-stack notification service. The project contribution is software engineering plus a transparent ML and RAG evaluation — not a claim to replace India’s statutory glanders programme or invent a new disease-control method.
